newsitem.title: USA: Body found with note to call Kevorkian's lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Body found with note to call Kevorkian's lawyer.

text.p: For the third time in a month, a body has turned up in a suburban Detroit hotel room accompanied by a note referring authorities to the lawyer of assisted suicide advocate Jack Kevorkian, police said Tuesday.

A security officer responding to an anonymous call entered a room at the Red Roof Inn in Warren and found the body of an elderly woman Monday night, Lt. Danny Clark of the Warren police department said.
"A note a been left in the room indicating personal information about the victim," Clark said. "Also in this note was information that Mr. (Geoffrey) Fieger is her representative."
Fieger, Kevorkian's longtime attorney and spokesman, was not available for comment on the incident Tuesday.
Clark said the death was being investigated as a suicide and said there were no "readily available signs of foul play."

Macomb County Prosecutor Karl Marlinga identified the woman as Janette Knowles, 75, of Norfolk, Nebraska, and said her note indicated that she suffered from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or Lou Gehrig's disease. She had a small puncture on her left arm, presumably from a hypodermic needle, but no syringes, drugs, fingerprints or other physical evidence was left in the room, he said.

"All we have is an indication that while alive this person retained as a lawyer Geoffrey Fieger," Marlinga said. "It is unlikely that we're going to get any information from Mr. Fieger as to what happened inside that room."
Even if Kevorkian were involved, Marlinga said he would not prosecute the 68-year-old retired pathologist because Michigan lacks a clear statute banning assisted suicide.

Knowles' death followed the same pattern as two other apparent suicides that referred authorities to Fieger. The body of Albert Miley, 43, of Warminster, Pennsylvania, was found March 19 in a motel room in Livonia, Michigan, and the body of Helen Livengood, 59, of Richmond, Virginia, was found in a Romulus, Michigan, hotel room March 7.

In each case Fieger said he represented the family of the victim and would not say if Kevorkian was involved in the deaths. He has hinted the assisted suicide activist had a role in the deaths of two other people, one of whom was found dead in Kevorkian's van, in February.

Kevorkian admitted being present at 45 deaths since 1990 but he has been silent on the issue since November, when he was released on $10,000 bond after promising to not be present at any more suicides.

He was arrested by Ionia, Michigan, authorities and charged with violating the state's unwritten "common law" that prohibits assisted suicide. The charges related to Kevorkian's role in helping Loretta Peabody, 54, of Ionia, die Aug. 30, 1996. Peabody suffered from multiple sclerosis.
Since 1994 Kevorkian has been acquitted in three assisted-suicide trials involving five deaths.
